extraction.name: BoolQ
extraction.description: BoolQ (Boolean Questions) is a reading comprehension dataset of naturally occurring yes/no questions. Each example consists of a question, a paragraph from a Wikipedia article, the title of the article, and an answer (yes or no). The questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine, and paired with Wikipedia passages that contain the answer. The dataset contains 16,000 questions split into 9.4k train, 3.2k dev, and 3.2k test sets.
extraction.creator: Christopher Clark, Kenton Lee, Ming-Wei Chang, Tom Kwiatkowski, Michael Collins, Kristina Toutanova
extraction.publisher: Paul G. Allen School of CSE, University of Washington; Google AI Language
extraction.citeAs: Clark, C., Lee, K., Chang, M.-W., Kwiatkowski, T., Collins, M., & Toutanova, K. (2019). BoolQ: Exploring the Surprising Difficulty of Natural Yes/No Questions. NAACL.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data was gathered using the pipeline from Natural Questions (NQ) with an additional filtering step to focus on yes/no questions. Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine. Queries likely to be yes/no questions are heuristically identified by selecting queries where the first word is in a manually constructed set of indicator words (did, do, does, is, are, was, were, have, has, can, could, will, would) and are of sufficient length. Questions are only kept if a Wikipedia page is returned as one of the first five results. The question and Wikipedia page are then given to a human annotator who labels in three steps: (1) decides if the question is good (comprehensible, unambiguous, requesting factual information), (2) finds a passage within the document containing enough information to answer, (3) marks whether the answer is yes or no. 13k questions gathered from this pipeline were combined with an additional 3k yes/no questions from the NQ training set.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Manual Human Curator, Passive Data Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine, paired with Wikipedia pages retrieved as search results. Additional yes/no questions were taken from the Natural Questions (NQ) training set.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Questions were heuristically filtered to identify yes/no questions based on the first word matching a manually constructed set of indicator words and sufficient length. Questions were only kept if a Wikipedia page appeared in the first five search results. Each question was paired with the annotator-selected passage (not the full document) to reduce ambiguity and keep input small enough for entailment models.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotators labeled question/article pairs in a three-step process: (1) decide if the question is 'good', meaning comprehensible, unambiguous, and requesting factual information (made before seeing the Wikipedia page); (2) for good questions, find a passage within the document that contains enough information to answer the question, or mark as 'not answerable' if the article doesn't contain the requested information; (3) mark whether the question's answer is 'yes' or 'no'. Annotation quality was assessed by having three of the authors label 110 randomly chosen examples, reaching 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard labels. Singly-annotated examples were used in train/dev/test sets to enable a larger dataset.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Three authors labeled 110 randomly chosen examples to create gold-standard labels (resolving disagreements by mutual agreement). The annotators' labels reached 90% accuracy compared to gold-standard. Of cases where the annotation differed from gold-standard, six were ambiguous/debatable cases, and five were errors where the annotator misunderstood the passage. Because agreement was sufficiently high, singly-annotated examples were used.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: 1 (singly-annotated); quality check used 3 annotators on 110 examples
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Questions are gathered from anonymized, aggregated queries to the Google search engine.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset is class imbalanced with 62.31% 'yes' answers in the training set (majority baseline). There is a correlation between the number of times question words occur in the passage and the answer being 'yes'. Passages that present more straightforward factual information (like Wikipedia introduction paragraphs) may correlate with 'yes' answers. Questions are biased toward topics people commonly search for (entertainment media, nature/science, sports, etc.).
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset pairs questions only with selected passages rather than full documents. Factoid questions asking about simple properties of entities are rare because people tend to phrase such questions as short-answer questions. Both passages and questions rarely include negation. The dataset is singly-annotated, so there may be some annotation errors (approximately 10% based on quality assessment). The majority baseline is 62.31%, and human accuracy is 90%, while best model achieves 80.43%, leaving a significant gap.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing machine learning models for reading comprehension and yes/no question answering. The dataset is used to test models' ability to make inferences from natural text, including paraphrasing, factual reasoning, by-example reasoning, implicit reasoning, and missing mention reasoning. Can be used as a source for transfer learning experiments.
